items.title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers
items.summary: On November 18, 2026, Hugging Face developer Tarek Ziadé detailed an experiment pushing Mixture of Experts (MoE) model inference to the limit using Transformers on a 32GB MacBook M5. Ziadé tackled the challenge of running massive models—specifically the 180-p…
items.fullStory:
On November 18, 2026, Hugging Face developer Tarek Ziadé detailed an experiment pushing Mixture of Experts (MoE) model inference to the limit using Transformers on a 32GB MacBook M5. Ziadé tackled the challenge of running massive models—specifically the 180-parameter Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model containing 121GB of experts—on consumer hardware with limited unified memory. By default, standard engines like llama.cpp, vLLM, and Transformers struggle with massive MoE offloading due to lack of caching, inefficient routing, or severe PCIe bottlenecks.

To bridge this gap, Ziadé developed a custom expert-streaming approach integrated into Hugging Face's Transformers via pull request #50717. The solution uses an LRU cache turned into a slot pool, allowing grouped matrix multiplication (grouped_mm) to run natively without custom expert kernels. Additionally, experts were quantized offline to 3 bits (reducing them to 49GB on disk with a 12 GiB device cache), dense layers were quantized to 8 bits, and the system utilized 8 I/O threads to prefetch experts by reading routers early.

After optimizations including Metal kernels, PyTorch MPS commit forcing, and adopting Strata's GGUF weights, the custom Transformers setup achieved impressive benchmark results on the 32GB Mac. It reached 13.9 tok/s on short decode (compared to Strata's 14.8 tok/s), 228 tok/s on a 4K prefill prompt, and 12.4 tok/s on decode after a 6K document. Ziadé noted that the remaining performance gap is largely due to host round trips and limitations in PyTorch's MPS stream regarding GPU and CPU synchronization.

Ziadé released the code in a Hugging Face Space called tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming and submitted the core changes to the official Transformers repository. Next steps involve discussing the API with Transformers maintainers, potentially merging quantized expert features into per-layer quantization plans, and addressing PyTorch MPS limitations.
items.whyItMatters: This breakthrough demonstrates that massive 180B parameter MoE models can run efficiently on consumer hardware like a 32GB Mac using standard tools like Transformers, significantly lowering the barrier for local AI development.
items.whoIsAffected: AI developers, researchers, and local hardware enthusiasts running large Mixture of Experts models on consumer devices.

items.title: Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages
items.summary: On November 18, 2026, researchers Reson8 (including contributors Reson8, Mark 't Hart, Eustache Le Bihan, and Eric Bezzam) open-sourced Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It is a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model designed for over 40 languages…
items.fullStory:
On November 18, 2026, researchers Reson8 (including contributors Reson8, Mark 't Hart, Eustache Le Bihan, and Eric Bezzam) open-sourced Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It is a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model designed for over 40 languages. The model features native support in 🤗 Transformers and vLLM without custom code, automatic language detection, and output control such as numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, and forced language.

Built using the Qwen3-ASR architecture, Rumble-2-Flash was created by distilling a larger production model, Rumble-2, using on-policy distillation combined with a technique called GOLD to bridge tokenizer differences between the teacher and student models. The creators tested how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off by having the student transcribe audio itself while the teacher graded transcripts token by token.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash achieved an average error rate of 6.96% across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch, and English, outperforming Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B and Whisper large-v3. It achieved 6.6% WER on the English track and processing speeds reaching over 7,000 RTFx on full batches, transcribing an hour of audio in about half a second. On AppTek's 302-hour call-centre benchmark featuring 14 English accents, it reached 7.86% WER, performing on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B).

The model weights are available on the Hugging Face Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash, and the model is also accessible through an API. The creators invited community feedback and project sharing in the Discussions tab.
items.whyItMatters: Rumble-2-Flash demonstrates that a tiny 0.5B-parameter speech model can match the performance of models up to 60 times its size while running exceptionally fast and efficiently on standard infrastructure.
items.whoIsAffected: Software developers, AI engineers, and enterprises building speech recognition and audio transcription applications.

items.title: Branch, sync, serve: What our Lakebase Hackathon taught us about building on Lakebase
items.summary: On November 17, 2026, Databricks published a field guide highlighting eleven customer projects from its latest Lakebase hackathon. The event focused on Databricks Lakebase, a fully managed Postgres database built for the lakehouse with separated storage and c…
items.fullStory:
On November 17, 2026, Databricks published a field guide highlighting eleven customer projects from its latest Lakebase hackathon. The event focused on Databricks Lakebase, a fully managed Postgres database built for the lakehouse with separated storage and compute, operating under Unity Catalog governance.

The hackathon was split into two main tracks: Track 1 centered on application development and database branching, while Track 2 concentrated on syncing data and real-time serving. Participants included teams from Lyft, CIBC, Arbital Health, OneTrust, Reach Mobile, Markel, Data Axle, and Sobeys. Notable projects included Lyft's 'Jevons Search'—which used copy-on-write branching to give AI agents a safe production copy for processing support tickets in about six seconds—and Data Axle's 'PriceWise', which utilized synced tables and pgvector embeddings to deliver vacation rental pricing suggestions in as little as 4 milliseconds.

Stated consequences and outcomes from the hackathon demonstrated how Lakebase eliminates the need for separate systems like auxiliary search indices or slow staging databases. Projects successfully replaced traditional setups by combining operational database capabilities with lakehouse governance, allowing teams to test schema changes, spin up preview environments in under five seconds, and unify analytics with real-time application serving.
items.whyItMatters: The Lakebase hackathon demonstrates how operational Postgres databases can be tightly integrated with the lakehouse and Unity Catalog governance, enabling real-time serving, instant branching, and streamlined application development without separate legacy systems.

items.title: Built on object storage, served from cache
items.summary: On November 17, 2026, Databricks Engineering published an overview detailing how Lakebase Postgres achieves high performance while relying on object storage for durability, branching, and transactional and analytical processing (LTAP). While object storage pr…
items.fullStory:
On November 17, 2026, Databricks Engineering published an overview detailing how Lakebase Postgres achieves high performance while relying on object storage for durability, branching, and transactional and analytical processing (LTAP). While object storage provides bottomless storage and instant restores, Carlota Soto noted that reading directly from it can introduce high latency. To counter this, the architecture uses a tiered caching strategy where object storage is kept off the critical read path for active workloads.

Production statistics from Databricks' fleet demonstrate the efficacy of this caching model. The compute node's local cache serves approximately 1.1 billion page accesses per second, accounting for 99.46% of total reads at memory-level latency. When local misses occur, requests move to a pageserver backed by local NVMe, handling about 6 million reads per second (0.54%). Only about 39 requests per second—roughly 1 in every 28 million page accesses, or over 99.99999%—ever reach object storage.

These rare object-storage reads typically occur under specific circumstances, such as accessing old historical branches, performing point-in-time restores, or waking up databases that have been idle for weeks. Once fetched, the data is immediately cached in the faster tiers. Furthermore, pageservers organize data into image layers and delta layers, with p90 metrics staying under 1 delta per GetPage read, ensuring that even off-compute reads avoid heavy replay chains.

The lakebase architecture decouples standard Postgres compute from a storage layer composed of safekeepers for WAL replication, pageservers for managing local NVMe and LSM trees, and object storage for long-term history. Next steps for the platform involve continuing to leverage this decoupled model to provide the cost and durability benefits of object storage without sacrificing traditional database performance.
items.whyItMatters: This architecture proves that Postgres can be successfully built on top of object storage without suffering from latency penalties, achieving over 99.99999% cache-hit efficiency. It redefines how cloud-native databases can combine bottomless storage with high-performance operational workloads.
items.whoIsAffected: Data architects, database administrators, and engineers building applications on Lakebase Postgres.
